question text: A shop sells a used phone in instalments. What must its invoice contain?
ground truth: On the consumer's request, a clear invoice at no extra charge showing: supplier and shop name; date; price; type, essential features and warranty period; that the product is used (its condition); quantity; delivery date; signature or stamp. For instalments it must also show the total instalment amount, the actual annual interest rate and how it is calculated, the date interest starts, the number and value of instalments, the instalment period, penalties for default or late payment, the parties' rights over ownership during the period, and the consumer's acknowledgement of these terms. [Doc 6, Art. 4, pp. 14-15]
answer:
When a shop sells a product—such as a used phone—in instalments, it must provide the consumer, upon request, with a clear and legible written invoice at no extra financial or non-financial cost [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)]. 

The invoice must include the following general details:
1. The supplier's name and commercial shop name [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
2. The date of the transaction or contract [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
3. The price of the product [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
4. The type of product, its essential characteristics, and the warranty period [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
5. A statement that the product is used (since it is a used phone) [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
6. The quantity of the product by number or weight [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
7. The delivery date of the product [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
8. The signature or stamp of the supplier or their legal representative [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].

Additionally, for instalment sales, the supplier must comply with the Central Bank of Bahrain and Financial Institutions Law No. 64 of 2006 and its regulations, and the invoice must contain these extra details:
1. The total instalment amount [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
2. The actual annual interest rate and how it is calculated [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
3. The date from which interest begins to be calculated [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
4. The number of instalments and the value of each instalment [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
5. The instalment period [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
6. The penalties imposed on the consumer for defaulting or delaying instalment payments [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
7. The rights and obligations of both contracting parties regarding the product's ownership and disposal during the instalment period [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].
8. Acknowledgment that the consumer has reviewed and accepted these additional details [Executive Regulation (MD 66/2014), Article 4 (pp. 14-15)].

notes: All 8 general and 8 instalment items, each cited to ER Art. 4 (the passage holds them).

question text: A shop advertised a television at a set price in a newspaper, then charged a higher price at the till. Which obligations does this breach and what penalty does the order refer to?
ground truth: Shops that announce retail prices must keep to them and must not manipulate them, especially at payment. Anyone advertising goods at a set price in newspapers or on roads must ensure the advertised price is actual and matches reality. Violators face the penalties in Decree-Law No. 18 of 1975 (as amended by Decree-Law No. 11 of 1977), as well as closure of the shop where the manipulation took place. [Doc 8, Art. 1-3, p. 7]
answer:
Charging a higher price at the till than the advertised price breaches the requirement that any advertised price for a good or service—whether in newspapers, roads, or public streets—must be actual, realistic, and free from any manipulative practices targeting consumers [MO 14/2008, Article 2 (p. 7)]. Shop and factory owners who announce retail prices must also strictly adhere to those advertised prices and avoid any price manipulation, particularly at the time of payment [MO 14/2008, Article 1 (p. 7)].

Regarding penalties, the order refers to the penalties stipulated in Decree-Law No. (18) of 1975 on fixing prices and price control, as amended by Decree-Law No. (11) of 1977, while taking into account the penalty of closing the business establishment where the price manipulation took place [MO 14/2008, Article 3 (p. 7)].

notes: Both obligations (Art. 1-2) and the penalty with shop closure (Art. 3), each cited correctly.

question text: How long does a supplier have to provide spare parts and maintenance after a consumer asks, and when is it released from this duty?
ground truth: Within at most 15 working days of the request. The parties may agree a specific period in writing. The supplier is released if it notifies the consumer in writing that the parts are unavailable and the consumer agrees. [Doc 6, Art. 16, p. 18; Doc 4, Art. 9, p. 6]
answer:
Suppliers must provide necessary spare parts and maintenance for a reasonable period proportionate to the product's nature, unless a specific period is agreed upon in writing with the consumer [Law 35/2012 (EN), Article 9 (p. 6)]. 

A supplier is released from this obligation if they give the consumer written notice that spare parts are unavailable for the product, and the consumer agrees to this [Law 35/2012 (EN), Article 9 (p. 6)].

question text: How did the Education index change between August and September 2025 and from then to August 2026, and what does iGA's method say about how often education prices are collected and their weight?
ground truth: It rose 2.8% from 108.41 to 111.4 in September 2025 and stayed at 111.4 every month to August 2026. iGA's method lists education, 8.6% of the basket weight, under annual price collection. [Dataset 1: code 10; Doc 9, section 5.3, pp. 7-8]
answer:
The national Education index rose 2.8% from August 2025 to September 2025, moving from an index level of 108.4 to 111.4 [iGA CPI Sep 2023, excerpt 1 (p. 8)]. From September 2025 to August 2026, the Education index did not change, remaining at 111.4 [iGA CPI Sep 2023, excerpt 1 (p. 8)]. (Percentage changes are the group's own calculations from iGA's index numbers, not official figures.)

According to iGA's CPI methodology, education prices are collected annually, and the education group accounts for 8.6% of the total weight of the CPI basket [iGA CPI Sep 2023, excerpt 1 (p. 8)].

question text: A customer changes their mind about a jacket bought yesterday that has no fault. Must the shop exchange it or give a refund?
ground truth: No, unless the shop's own policy offers it, in which case the shop must keep to that policy. The legal right to exchange or refund applies only where goods have a defect or fault or do not conform to the approved specifications or the purpose of the contract. The Ministry's guidance lists a change of mind, finding the item cheaper elsewhere, a defect the consumer was told of at purchase, and damage from misuse as cases with no refund or replacement. [Doc 10, PDF pp. 7-8; Doc 6, Art. 14, pp. 17-18]
answer:
A shop is not required to exchange or refund a jacket simply because a customer changed their mind, provided the item has no defect [Know Your Right (MOIC guidance), excerpt 1 (p. 8)]. 

According to consumer guidance, a consumer cannot expect a refund or replacement if they change their mind, did not benefit from using the item, find it cheaper elsewhere, were notified of a defect at purchase, or damaged the item through misuse [Know Your Right (MOIC guidance), excerpt 1 (p. 8)]. A right to a replacement or refund with return of the price at no additional cost applies only when goods have a defect, do not conform to approved specifications, or do not suit the purpose for which the contract was entered into [Know Your Right (MOIC guidance), excerpt 1 (p. 8)]. 

*(Note: This guidance dates from 2016.)*
notes: Core answer (no duty to exchange or refund for a change of mind) is right and cited to the 2016 guidance. Missing: the ground truth's 'unless the shop's own policy offers it' (guidance p. 7) and the legal basis in ER Art. 14; only 1 passage passed the 0.40 minimum score.
